objective: By the end of this lesson you can decide at the DA, MDA or VDP whether 14 CFR 91.175 lets you go lower, read the approach lights, VASI or PAPI and runway markings, and fly a stabilized visual descent to a normal landing, or go around when it is not safe.
why: The last few hundred feet of an instrument approach are where you switch from the panel to the outside world, often in rain, haze or darkness. Flying low, fast or unstable there leads to landing short, landing long and losing control.

prereading.what: Authorized DA/MDA, the three tests for going below it, landing visibility, missed approach triggers and the RVR conversion table.

warmup: You reach the MDA at night in light rain and see a few bright lights ahead, but you are not sure they are the runway. What would you need to see, and how sure would you need to be, before you descend any lower?

key_terms.def: Altitude (MSL) on a vertically guided approach where you go missed unless you see the required visual reference.
Lowest altitude (MSL) on a nonprecision or circling approach until you see the required visual references.
Point on a straight-in nonprecision final, marked (V), where a stabilized descent from the MDA to the runway can begin.
The part of the approach from the DA or MDA down to the runway, flown by outside visual references.
Average forward distance from the cockpit at which you can see and identify prominent objects. Only you can judge it.
Pattern of lights extending from the threshold into the approach area. The main aid for the switch to visual.
Visual glidepath lights beside the runway. Red and white combinations show high, on or low.
Highest elevation in the first 3,000 ft of the landing surface. HAT and the 100 ft approach light limit are measured from it.
Constant glidepath, airspeed, descent rate and configuration toward the touchdown point, with only small corrections.
Small, intense downdraft that spreads out at the surface, giving headwind, then downdraft, then tailwind.
Any occurrence at an airport where an aircraft, vehicle or person is wrongly on the protected area of a runway.

chunks.title: The visual segment: from DA or MDA to the runway

body.p: A decision altitude (DA) is where you must decide: go missed if you do not see the required visual reference, or continue [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]]. A minimum descent altitude (MDA) is the lowest altitude you may descend to on final or while circling until you see the required visual references [[60:10|14 CFR 1.1]].

The visual segment begins at the DA or MDA and goes to the runway. You fly it with natural vision under 91.175(c), or with an enhanced flight vision system (EFVS) under 91.176 [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. This lesson covers natural vision.

Approach lights are the basic means of moving from instrument flight to visual flight for landing [[33:121|AIM 2-1-1]]. Once you descend below the DA or MDA, you are also the one who must see and avoid obstacles. There is no built-in obstacle protection from the MDA or DA to the touchdown point [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

head: Term
How it is measured
Where you meet it
rows: ILS, LPV, LNAV/VNAV: decide at the DA
Feet AGL; CAT II and III use a radio altimeter [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]
LNAV, LOC, VOR and circling: level off and look
DME or RNAV distance to the MAP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]

callout.text: Your authorized DA or MDA is the highest of three: the one on the chart, the one set for you as pilot in command, and the one allowed by the equipment you actually use [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

check.q: Who is responsible for clearing obstacles between the MDA and the runway?
check.a: You are. There is no implicit obstacle protection below the MDA or DA, so you must see and avoid obstacles in the visual segment [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

chunks.title: 91.175(c): the three tests for going lower

body.p: You may not go below the MDA, or continue below the DA, unless all three of these are true [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]:

bullets: 1. You are continuously in a position to descend to a landing on the intended runway at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].
2. The flight visibility is not less than the visibility on the approach chart [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]].
3. At least one of the listed visual references for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

head: Visual references in 91.175(c)(3)
rows: Approach light system, but not below 100 ft above TDZE on the approach lights alone, unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also distinctly visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]
Threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]]
Touchdown zone or its markings, touchdown zone lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]]
Runway or runway markings, runway lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]]

callout.text: Three tests: POSITION (normal descent, normal maneuvers), VISIBILITY (flight visibility at or above the chart), REFERENCE (one of the ten, for the runway you will land on). Approach lights alone get you to 100 ft above TDZE, no lower, unless you see red bars [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]].

body.p: Flight visibility is the average forward distance from the cockpit at which you can see and identify prominent unlighted objects by day and lighted objects by night [[60:7|14 CFR 1.1]]. ATC gives you reported visibility, RVR or prevailing visibility, but only you can judge flight visibility. If it is below the chart value, go missed regardless of the report [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

You also may not land if the flight visibility is less than the visibility in the approach you are flying [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]]. Go missed right away if the 91.175(c) tests are not met while below the MDA, or at the missed approach point (including the DA) and any time after until touchdown [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

Use this table when an RVR minimum is published but RVR is not reported for your runway [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(h)(1)]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)(2)]]. For RVR values between those listed, use the next higher RVR value; do not interpolate. 1,800 RVR becomes 2,400 RVR, or 1/2 mile [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]].

check.q: At the MDA you see the approach lights, but there are no red terminating or side row bars. How low may you go on those lights alone?
check.a: To 100 ft above the touchdown zone elevation. Below that you need another reference, such as the threshold or runway lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

body.p: An approach light system (ALS) is a pattern of lights that starts at the landing threshold and extends into the approach area: 2,400 to 3,000 ft for precision instrument runways and 1,400 to 1,500 ft for nonprecision runways [[33:121|AIM 2-1-1]]. Some have sequenced flashing lights that look like a ball of light racing toward the runway twice a second, often called "the rabbit" [[33:121|AIM 2-1-1]] [[23:281|IFH 9-38]].

The ALS gives you direction, distance and glidepath information far enough out to make a safe visual transition [[23:281|IFH 9-38]]. Look for red. In the FAA figures only two systems show red lights: the ALSF-2 has rows of red on each side of the centerline near the threshold, and the ALSF-1 has short red bars just before the threshold. SSALR/MALSR and MALSF show none [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]] [[33:122|AIM FIG 2-1-1]]. These are the red side row bars and red terminating bars of the 100 ft rule [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. A civil ALSF-2 may be run as an SSALR in good weather, and an SSALR shows no red [[33:122|AIM FIG 2-1-1]].

REIL are a pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the threshold. They help you find a runway surrounded by other lights, a runway that blends into the terrain, or a runway in low visibility [[33:126|AIM 2-1-3]].

callout.text: Recognizing the ALS must be instant, so know which system you will see before you start the approach. Check the approach chart and the Chart Supplement [[23:281|IFH 9-38]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

body.p: Minimums assume all the approach's components and visual aids are working. If approach lights or another component are out, higher minimums apply [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. Read the chart notes and NOTAMs first, then the current TPP guidance the AIM points to [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j REFERENCE]]. Don't memorize numbers from an old printed table.

callout.text: Pilot-controlled lighting: key the mike 7 times within 5 seconds first, for the highest intensity, then 5 or 3 times to lower it. Lights stay on 15 minutes from the last activation, so key again just before the final segment [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

check.q: You fly an ILS to a runway with a MALSR. At DA you see only the approach lights. Is that enough to continue, and to where?
check.a: Yes, you may continue below DA, but only to 100 ft above TDZE on the approach lights alone, because a MALSR shows no red side row or terminating bars [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]] [[33:122|AIM FIG 2-1-1]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

chunks.title: Visual glidepath lights: VASI and PAPI

body.p: A VASI uses red and white beams. A two-bar VASI gives one glidepath, normally 3°, though some are as steep as 4.5° for obstacle clearance [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]]. VASI lights are visible 3 to 5 miles by day and 20 miles or more at night [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]].

callout.text: VASI: red over white, you're all right. Red over red, you're dead (too low). White over white, you'll fly all night (too high). Below the glidepath, a distinct all-red signal means safe obstacle clearance might not exist [[23:281|IFH 9-38]].

body.p: A PAPI is a single row of two or four lights, normally on the left side of the runway. It is visible about 5 miles by day and up to 20 miles at night [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].

head: Light system
Clearance area or useful range
Notes
rows: ±10° of the extended centerline, out to 4 NM [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]]
Do not start the descent until you are visually lined up with the runway [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]]
±10° of the extended centerline, out to 3.4 NM [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]]
The area may be narrowed or the lights offset; this is in the Chart Supplement or NOTAMs [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]]
Useful range 1/2 to 1 mile by day, up to 5 miles at night [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2c]]
Red below, green on, amber above. A single light can be confused with other lights [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2c]]
About 4 miles by day, 10 at night [[33:125|AIM 2-1-2d]]
Steady red slightly low, pulsing red lower, pulsing white high [[33:125|AIM 2-1-2d]]

body.p: Lateral guidance comes from the runway or runway lights, not the VASI or PAPI [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]]. On a nonprecision approach you can use the VGSI to judge if you are in position for a stabilized descent from the MDA, but near minimum visibility it may not be visible from the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

callout.text: Some charts say "Straight-in Rwy XX at Night, operational VGSI required, remain on or above VGSI glidepath until threshold." That is a procedure restriction, not advice [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

check.q: A four-light PAPI shows three red and one white. Where are you?
check.a: Slightly low, about 2.8°. Two red and two white is on the 3° glidepath [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]].

chunks.title: The runway environment: markings, lights and signs

body.p: Runway markings are white. Taxiway markings and holding positions, even on a runway, are yellow [[33:138|AIM 2-3-2b]]. A precision instrument runway has the most markings:

bullets: Threshold markings: the beginning of the runway available for landing [[33:140|AIM 2-3-3h]].
Aiming point marking: two broad white stripes about 1,000 ft from the threshold [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3d]].
Touchdown zone markings: pairs of one, two and three bars that give distance in 500 ft steps [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3e]].

Displaced threshold: a 10 ft white bar across the runway, with white arrows before it. You may not land on the area behind it, though you may take off there or land on it from the opposite direction [[33:141|AIM 2-3-3h2]].

head: Lights
What they tell you
rows: White. On instrument runways yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less: a caution zone [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]
Green toward you as you land (threshold), red toward a departing airplane (end of runway) [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]
White until the last 3,000 ft, then alternating red and white for 2,000 ft, then all red for the last 1,000 ft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]]
Two rows of white light bars from 100 ft past the threshold to 3,000 ft or the runway midpoint, whichever is less [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5b]]
Pulsing white lights across the runway at the LAHSO hold short point, on when LAHSO is in effect [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5e]]

body.p: Runway distance remaining signs are black with white numbers showing thousands of feet of runway left [[33:172|AIM 2-3-13]]. Holding position markings (two solid and two dashed yellow lines) also mark where you are clear after landing: you are not clear until all parts of the airplane have crossed them [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]].

callout.text: Brief the runway environment before the approach: lighting type, VGSI side and angle, displaced threshold, runway length and width, slope. The Chart Supplement and airport diagram have it [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

check.q: On rollout at night the runway edge lights turn yellow. What does that mean?
check.a: You are in the caution zone: the last 2,000 ft of an instrument runway, or the last half if that is less [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]].

chunks.title: Landing profiles: straight-in, VDP and circling

body.p: **Vertically guided approaches** (ILS, LPV, LNAV/VNAV) help the transition because you are already stabilized on the glidepath when you see the runway [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Just stay on it.

**Nonprecision straight-in.** Use a descent rate that gets you to the MDA far enough out to land in the touchdown zone. On many approaches that point is the VDP [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Do not descend below the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. If you can't identify the VDP, fly the approach as if there were none [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

head: Rule of thumb
How
IPH example
rows: Height above TDZE = NM from threshold × 300
Where to leave the MDA (no VDP)
Height above TDZE ÷ 300 = NM from threshold

callout.text: Between the VDP and the MAP, a descent from the MDA may be inadvisable or impossible. Speed, height, descent rate, amount of turn and runway length decide if you can still land safely [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. If the MAP is at the threshold of a short runway, arriving there at the MDA usually means a missed approach [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

body.p: **Straight-in vs circling.** Straight-in minimums are published only when the final course is within 30° of the runway and a normal descent is possible. You may still land straight-in with the runway in sight, time for a normal approach and a landing clearance [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

**Circling.** Stay at or above the circling MDA until you are continuously in position to descend at a normal rate with normal maneuvers [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]]. If the ceiling allows, fly closer to VFR pattern altitude; it makes maneuvering safer and the runway look normal [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. Stay inside the circling area and obey circling restrictions; an ATC clearance does not cancel them [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

callout.text: While circling at or above MDA, go missed if an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible, unless only a normal bank hides it [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Make the first climbing turn toward the landing runway, then intercept the missed approach course [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

check.q: MDA 1,040 ft MSL, TDZE 440 ft, no VDP published. About how far from the threshold should you leave the MDA?
check.a: Height above TDZE is 600 ft. 600 ÷ 300 = 2 NM [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

body.p: A stabilized approach keeps speed, descent rate, flight path and configuration constant in the final stages. It makes the decision at the DA or MAP much easier [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. The AFH lists these criteria for a typical piston airplane [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]:

head: Item
Stabilized means
rows: A constant 3° to the touchdown zone, obstructions permitting
Tracking the centerline with only small corrections; bank normally 15° or less on final
Within +10/-5 knots of the recommended landing speed (AFM, 1.3 VSO or placard)
Landing configuration: flaps as required, gear down, in trim
Generally 500 to 1,000 fpm. If over 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 ft AGL
Right for the configuration, not below the AFM minimum for approach
All done before the approach, except the landing checklist

callout.text: Go around if you are not stabilized by 1,000 ft above airport elevation in IMC (500 ft in VMC). In a typical GA piston airplane, go around immediately if the approach becomes unstable below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Descent rates above about 1,000 fpm are unacceptable below 1,000 ft AGL, in both the instrument and visual parts of the approach. That is a human perception limit, not an airplane limit [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Limit configuration changes at low altitude to ones you can handle easily [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

**Reading the runway.** On a stabilized approach the runway keeps the same shape as it grows [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. If it seems to get shorter and wider, you are getting shallow. If it gets longer and narrower, you are getting steep [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

bullets: Too high: reduce power and lower the nose to hold airspeed; add flaps if available [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Too low: add power and raise the nose to level off until you meet the glide path. Never raise flaps to fix an undershoot; it can cause a sudden sink [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Gusty winds: add one-half the gust factor. Normal 70 knots with 15 knot gusts: about 77 knots. Use partial flaps in gusty crosswinds, and follow the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

check.q: On short final you are low and slow. Your instinct is to raise the flaps to stretch the glide. Why not?
check.a: Retracting flaps to fix an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift and a high sink rate. Add power and pitch instead [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: At the end of an instrument approach you switch from instruments to outside cues, and that is exactly when optical illusions strike. Most of them affect landing [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

head: Illusion
What you think
What you tend to fly
rows: You are higher than you are
Too low: hit objects or land short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]
You are lower than you are
Too high: level off high, land hard or long [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]
Featureless terrain: water, dark areas, snow ("black hole")
Farther from the runway than you are
Bright runway lights, few lights around
Closer to the runway than you are

body.p: Lights along a straight road, or even on a moving train, can be mistaken for runway or approach lights [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5b3(f)]]. That is why 91.175(c) says the reference must be distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

callout.text: Prevent illusion errors: expect them at unfamiliar airports, at night and in bad weather; study the Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting; check the altimeter often; use VASI, PAPI or the electronic glideslope; and use the VDP [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

check.q: Night approach over dark woods to a lighted runway, in light rain. Which way will the illusions push you, and what do you do?
check.a: Low. Featureless terrain and rain both make you feel higher than you are [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Stay on the glideslope or VGSI and cross-check the altimeter [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

chunks.title: Wind shear, wake turbulence and ATC advisories

body.p: Wind shear is a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area. Low-level wind shear is the most dangerous because you are close to the ground. Look for it with fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and strong upper winds over 25 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: Tailwind changing to headwind: airspeed and performance go up [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Headwind changing to tailwind: airspeed and performance go down [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
A microburst can produce downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots. It is 1 to 2 miles across and lasts 5 to 15 minutes [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

body.p: On approach, a microburst gives you a headwind (you balloon high and fast), then a downdraft, then a tailwind, and can force you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Microbursts can come from benign-looking cells with little rain and are hard to detect [[34:107|AIM 7-1-24]].

**Reporting.** Don't say "negative" or "positive" wind shear. Say the airspeed gain or loss and the altitude: "Cessna 1234 encountered wind shear, loss of 20 knots at 400" [[34:106|AIM 7-1-22]] [[34:107|AIM 7-1-22]]. If you fly a wind shear escape, tell ATC once the airplane is under control [[34:107|AIM 7-1-22c]].

**Wake turbulence.** Landing behind a larger airplane on the same runway: stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Behind a larger airplane that is departing: land well before its rotation point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. You are expected to adjust your path whether or not ATC warns you [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

**NOTAMs and the runway.** NOTAMs tell you about a relocated threshold (for example "10/28 W 900 CLSD") [[33:141|AIM 2-3-3h1]], a VASI or PAPI that is offset or has a smaller clearance area [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]], and closed runways and taxiways [[7:3|AC 91-73B 7b(1)(c)]].

callout.text: Tell ATC when an instruction would make your approach unstable because of speed or descent rate [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]]. Accepting a "keep your speed up" you can't safely bleed off is how long, fast landings begin.

check.q: On a 2 mile final your airspeed jumps 15 knots and you balloon above the glidepath, near a rain shaft. What might come next?
check.a: A microburst: the headwind is followed by a downdraft and a tailwind that can drive you into the ground short of the runway. Be ready to go around [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

chunks.title: Landing distance and the runway surface

body.p: POH/AFM landing distances assume you cross the threshold at 50 ft, at the right speed, and touch down within the flight test air distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]]. A sloppy final quickly uses up the margin.

head: Factor
Effect on landing distance
rows: Each 10 ft above the 50 ft threshold height
About 200 ft longer; 100 ft over the threshold adds 1,000 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]
About 5% faster landing speed and 10% longer distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.6]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.6]]
Higher true airspeed and groundspeed, so longer [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.5]]

body.p: **Arrival check.** Before descent, compare the runway with your landing distance for the actual conditions, and add at least 15% safety margin [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. If your POH has only dry, unfactored data, AC 91-79B gives multipliers that already include the 15%. For a reciprocating airplane on a dry runway, multiply by 1.67; it is larger for contaminated runways, up to 5.1 with poor braking [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

Use the worst reliable braking report and note how old it is. Several overruns happened when a runway report was no longer valid because the weather had changed [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.3]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B 3.4.1]]. Decide before the approach how much worse the runway can get before you divert [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.1]].

callout.text: Fast, high or long: each one eats runway. 10% fast = 20% longer. 50 ft too high = 1,000 ft longer. 10 knots tailwind = 21% longer [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]].

check.q: Your POH dry landing distance is 1,400 ft. Using the AC 91-79B dry factor, what distance should the runway beat?
check.a: 1,400 × 1.67 = about 2,340 ft, which includes the 15% safety margin [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: from the approach to clear of the runway

body.p: **Before the approach**

bullets: 1. Review weather, NOTAMs, the airport diagram and runway data. Check fuel for a missed approach or diversion [[29:146|IPH 4-6]] [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

2. Brief: authorized DA or MDA [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]], VDP, ALS type and VGSI [[23:281|IFH 9-38]], and the missed approach [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Finish checklists early so you can focus on the approach [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].
3. Plan the landing distance and the go-around triggers before you need them [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.1]].

body.p: **From final approach fix to DA or MDA**

bullets: 4. Be in landing configuration and stabilized by 1,000 ft above the airport. Complete the landing checklist [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

5. Single pilot: keep flying by instruments while you look for the runway. Both jobs need you, so split your attention carefully [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Glance out, then back to the attitude indicator, and do not stop the scan.
6. At the DA, or at the MDA before the VDP: check the three tests of 91.175(c). If any one fails, go missed now [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

body.p: **Visual segment and landing**

bullets: 7. Continue on the glideslope or VGSI. On a nonprecision approach leave the MDA at the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. Keep the descent rate normal and do not dive for the runway [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
8. Hold the aiming point steady in the windshield and scan from it to the horizon and back [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Keep checking airspeed.
9. If anything goes wrong below the DA or MDA (visibility lost, runway out of sight, unstable, a vehicle on the runway) go around [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].
10. Touch down in the touchdown zone, then exit at the first available taxiway or as ATC says. Do not exit onto another runway without ATC authorization [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21a]].
11. Stop only once all parts of the airplane are past the holding position markings. Do no after-landing checklist items until then [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21b]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]].

callout.text: SRM means using every resource inside and outside the airplane: ATC, automation, checklists and your planning [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. A good autopilot on the approach frees your eyes for the runway search, but you still decide at the DA.

body.p: The ACS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task. The examiner wants a timely, legal decision at the DA, MDA or VDP, a stabilized visual descent, positive control to a stop, and compliance with advisories and checklists (ACS IR.VI.E.S1 to S5).

check.q: You touch down and the tower says nothing about where to exit. Where do you stop?
check.a: Exit at the first available taxiway and taxi until all parts of the airplane are past the runway holding position markings, then hold for instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

chunks.title: Risk: unstable, low, the switch to visual, and configuration

head: Hazard
Why it hurts
Mitigation
rows: Deviations in speed, altitude, descent rate or glideslope make recovery to the right path unlikely and raise overrun risk [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]]
Use the AFH criteria and go around if not stabilized by 1,000 ft in IMC [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Below the VASI glidepath, all red, obstacle clearance might not exist [[23:281|IFH 9-38]]. Illusions push you low [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]
Stay on the glideslope or VGSI to the threshold; never leave the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]
Shallow fog may leave too little visibility to flare. Single pilot is the hardest case [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]
Keep an instrument cross-check until the runway is clear and certain; be ready to go around [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]
Big speed and configuration changes late in the approach hurt awareness and the decision at minimums [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]
Be configured and trimmed, on a stabilized approach, by 1,000 ft above the airport in IMC [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]

body.p: **Why pilots don't go around.** The AFH names two reasons: landing expectancy (the belief that this one will work out) and pride (thinking a go-around is a failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. A go-around is a normal maneuver. It becomes dangerous only when delayed or done badly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Go-around: POWER, ATTITUDE, CONFIGURATION. Full allowable power smoothly and right away, then pitch, then clean up [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

body.p: A missed approach that starts below the MDA, past the MAP, may not have published obstacle clearance. The missed approach protects you only when it begins at or above the MAP and you climb at least 200 ft per NM [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. Before the approach, think about what you would do for a balked landing below the DA or MDA [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

callout.text: A wrong configuration also goes the other way: in a go-around, flaps or gear left down, or abrupt power, lead to a poor climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Know your airplane's go-around flap steps from the POH.

check.q: Name the two attitudes the AFH says delay go-arounds.

bullets: Descending below the MDA before the VDP, or diving for the runway at the MAP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]] [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
Using the approach lights below 100 ft above TDZE without seeing red bars or another reference [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].
Taking a road or other line of lights for the runway [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5b3(f)]].
Failure to complete the landing checklist in a timely manner [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Unstable approach; poor trim; trying to reach the runway with elevator alone [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Failure to compensate for flap extension [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Focusing too close (high round out) or too far (low round out) [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Excess airspeed at touchdown, or touching down while drifting [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
Failure to recognize a reason to go around, indecision and delay [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Excessive braking and loss of control on rollout [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

check.q: Why is "trying to reach the runway with elevator alone" an error when you are low?
check.a: Pitch alone trades airspeed for a moment; without power you get slower and sink more. It is on the AFH common errors list [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Add power and pitch together [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: where the lights are shown

body.p: Check the lights before you start down, because they are one of the visual references you may use. The middle briefing strip has an approach lighting system box with the name and an icon, such as ALSF-2 or MALSR. When a chart has straight-in minimums for parallel runways, it may list more than one system [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]]. The DFW 17C chart lists ALSF-2 for runway 17C and MALSR for 17R [[29:185|IPH Figure 4-24]].

Then read the airport sketch. Notes at the bottom give the runway lights, for example HIRL, TDZL and RCLS, and the REIL runways. Approach light icons sit on the side of the runway where they are installed. Symbols shown in negative mean pilot-controlled lighting, and an L symbol shows that the pilot can turn the airport lights on [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

Now use the lights. Under the regulation you may go below the DA or MDA only if the flight visibility is enough and at least one listed reference is distinctly visible. The list includes the approach lights, the threshold, its markings or lights, the REIL, the visual glideslope indicator, the touchdown zone, its markings or lights, and the runway, its markings or lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

There is one limit. If the approach lights are your only reference, you may not go below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation unless the red terminating bars or the red side row bars are also in sight [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. A chart note may raise the visibility when a light system is out, so read the notes before you fly.

f1.caption: Figure 9-36. Precision and nonprecision ALS configuration.
f1.alt: Six green panels showing approach light patterns leading to a runway threshold: ALSF-2 with long red side row bars beside a white centerline and crossbar, ALSF-1 with short red terminating bars near the threshold, SSALR/MALSR with white bars and flashers and no red, MALSF with white bars, a row of green lights across the middle and flashers, REIL with two flashing lights angled 10 and 15 degrees at the threshold, and ODALS with omnidirectional flashers. A legend shows flashing, steady and omnidirectional lights and spells out each abbreviation.

f2.caption: Figure 9-37. Standard two-bar VASI.
f2.alt: Three views of runway 25 with a two-bar VASI beside it: below glidepath both far and near bars red; on glidepath far bar red over near bar white; above glidepath both bars white.

f3.caption: FIG 2-1-5. Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI).
f3.alt: Five PAPI pictures next to a runway outline: four white lights, high (more than 3.5 degrees); three white and one red, slightly high (3.2 degrees); two white and two red, on glide path (3 degrees); one white and three red, slightly low (2.8 degrees); four red, low (less than 2.5 degrees).

f4.caption: FIG 2-3-1. Precision Instrument Runway Markings.
f4.alt: Diagram of runway 20L from the threshold: threshold markings in configuration A (eight stripes) and B (stripes by runway width), the designation 20 L, side stripes, centerline, touchdown zone markings of three, two and one bar pairs and the broad aiming point marking.

f5.caption: Figure 9-36. Precision and nonprecision ALS configuration (detail, system names hidden).
f5.alt: Upper part of four approach light panels without their names: the first with long red side row bars beside a white centerline and a white crossbar, a green threshold row and sequenced flashers; the second with short red terminating bars near the green threshold row; the third with white bars only and flashers farther out; the fourth with white bars and a green row of lights.

f6.caption: Figure 17-7. Runway illusions.
f6.alt: Side and pilot's-eye views: a narrower runway makes the airplane fly a red path below the yellow normal approach; a wider runway makes it fly above. A downsloping runway leads to a higher approach and an upsloping runway to a lower approach. Text boxes explain each illusion.

f7.caption: Figure 12-17. Effects of a microburst wind.
f7.alt: A strong downdraft from a cloud spreads out at the ground as outflow. An airplane departing meets an increasing headwind (1) and climbs above its path, then the downdraft (2), then an increasing tailwind (3), and sinks close to the ground (4) far below the green intended path.

f8.caption: Figure 4-24 (detail). Top briefing strip of the DFW ILS or LOC RWY 17C chart.
f8.alt: Top part of the DFW ILS or LOC RWY 17C chart. The first strip gives LOC/DME I-FLQ 110.3, approach course 174, and runway landing data for 17C and 17R. The middle strip has a note box, then two lighting boxes: Rwy 17C ALSF-2 with a circled A icon and Rwy 17R MALSR with a circled A5 icon, then the missed approach text in yellow. Below are the ATIS, approach, tower, ground and clearance delivery frequencies.

f9.caption: Airport sketch with lighting notes.
f9.alt: Airport sketch box with elevation 143 and a D symbol. Runways 10-28, 15R-33L and 15L-33R have circled approach light symbols (A and A5) at their ends. Notes below read TDZL/RCLS Rwys 10 and 33L, REIL Rwys 15L and 33R and HIRL all rwys. A FAF to MAP table for 3.5 NM runs from 3:30 at 60 knots to 1:10 at 180 knots.

scenario.title: Night LNAV approach to a narrow runway in rain
scenario.setup: You fly an RNAV (GPS) RWY 27 approach at night to a small airport surrounded by dark farmland. LNAV MDA is 1,060 ft MSL, TDZE 460 ft, visibility minimum 1 SM, VDP 2.0 NM from the threshold. Runway 27 is 4,000 ft by 75 ft (you usually land on 150 ft wide runways), with a MALSR and a 4-light PAPI on the left. AWOS: wind 300 at 12 gusting 20, visibility 1 1/2 SM in light rain, ceiling 700 overcast. Your POH landing speed is 65 knots, and the dry landing distance over a 50 ft obstacle is 1,350 ft.

questions.q: You level at the MDA 3 NM out and see the MALSR right away. Can you start down now?
questions.a: No. Do not descend below the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. At the VDP you may continue on the approach lights if flight visibility is at least 1 SM and you can descend normally [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. A MALSR has no red bars, so you need another reference, such as the threshold, runway lights or PAPI, before going below 560 ft MSL (100 ft above TDZE) [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

questions.q: Past the VDP the runway looks normal, but the PAPI shows four red. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.a: You are low, below about 2.5° [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]]. Dark terrain, rain on the windscreen and a narrow runway all make you feel higher than you are, so you drift low [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5b3(e)]]. Add power and pitch to level off until you are back on the glidepath; don't use flaps to fix it [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. If you can't fix it with small corrections before 300 ft AGL, go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: What approach speed do you fly with the gusts?
questions.a: Add one-half the gust factor: gusts are 8 knots above the steady wind, so add 4. Fly about 69 knots, within the AFM/POH limits [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

questions.q: Is the 4,000 ft runway long enough if it is wet?
questions.a: On a dry runway the AC 91-79B factor gives 1,350 × 1.67 = about 2,255 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. Wet and with gusts adds more, and being 10% fast adds about 20% [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. The runway is likely fine, but only if you cross the threshold near 50 ft at the right speed; 100 ft over the threshold adds about 1,000 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

questions.q: At 300 ft AGL heavier rain hides the runway lights. You still see the approach lights. What now?
questions.a: Below the MDA, if the 91.175(c) requirements are not met, you must go missed right away [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. Go around: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. You are below the MDA and before the MAP, so the published missed approach does not protect you yet: it assumes you start at or above the MAP [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. Climb, fly the approach course to the MAP and only then turn, unless ATC clears you otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

skills.do: At the DA/DH, MDA or VDP, decide correctly whether 91.175(c) allows you to continue, then make a stabilized visual descent and a normal landing in the touchdown zone. The ACS sets no numeric tolerance; the examiner looks for a legal, timely decision (ACS IR.VI.E.S1).
skills.practice: On each training approach, call out the three tests aloud at minimums: position, visibility, reference [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. Practice leaving the MDA at the VDP and holding the VGSI to the threshold [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

skills.do: Follow ATC or evaluator advisories, including NOTAMs, wind shear, wake turbulence and runway surface conditions, and adjust the approach and landing (ACS IR.VI.E.S2).
skills.practice: Before each approach, brief the NOTAMs, wake turbulence plan and landing distance with a safety margin [[33:141|AIM 2-3-3h1]] [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. Practice a wind shear PIREP: airspeed change and altitude [[34:106|AIM 7-1-22]].

skills.do: Complete the approach, before-landing and after-landing checklists at the right times (ACS IR.VI.E.S3).
skills.practice: Finish briefings and checklists before the approach, the landing checklist by 1,000 ft [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and after-landing items only once clear of the hold line [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]].

skills.do: Keep positive control through the transition, flare, touchdown and rollout, including gusts and crosswind (ACS IR.VI.E.S4).
skills.practice: Fly the AFH stabilized criteria: +10/-5 knots, 500 to 1,000 fpm, centerline tracking [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Add half the gust factor in gusty air [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

skills.do: Use SRM or CRM: organize the cockpit, use automation and ATC well, and make the go-around decision without delay (ACS IR.VI.E.S5).
skills.practice: Plan resources before flight so you can act with crew-like efficiency [[30:57|RMH 8-4]]. With an instructor, practice calls like "minimums, runway in sight" or "minimums, going missed" [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

quiz.q: At the DA you see the approach lights only. The system has no red terminating or side row bars. How far may you descend?
options: To 100 ft above the touchdown zone elevation
To touchdown, if flight visibility is at minimums
To 200 ft above the touchdown zone elevation
Not at all; approach lights alone never count
quiz.why: Approach lights count as a reference, but you may not go below 100 ft above TDZE on them unless red terminating or side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 91.175(c)(3) visual references?
options: The airport rotating beacon
Touchdown zone markings
Runway end identifier lights
The visual glideslope indicator
quiz.why: REIL, touchdown zone markings and the VGSI are on the list. The airport beacon is not a reference for the intended runway [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

quiz.q: A four-light PAPI shows one white and three red. You are:
options: Slightly high, about 3.2°
On the glidepath, 3°
Slightly low, about 2.8°
Low, below 2.5°
quiz.why: One white and three red is slightly low (2.8°); two and two is on path; four red is low [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]].

quiz.q: A VASI provides safe obstruction clearance within what area?
options: ±35° of the centerline out to 10 NM
±10° of the centerline out to 4 NM
±10° of the centerline out to 10 NM
Only inside the runway threshold
quiz.why: The VASI glide path clears obstructions within ±10° of the extended centerline and out to 4 NM from the threshold [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]].

quiz.q: On an instrument runway, what does a yellow runway edge light mean?
options: A taxiway crosses or joins the runway ahead of you
You are on the displaced threshold, before the landing zone
The runway is closed beyond this point; do not land
You are in the last 2,000 ft or last half of the runway
quiz.why: Yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less, as a caution zone [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]].

quiz.q: The runway is much narrower than you are used to. Without correction you tend to:
options: Fly a higher approach and risk floating down the runway
Level off too high above the runway and land hard
Fly a lower approach and risk landing short
Drift toward the left edge of the runway on short final
quiz.why: A narrow runway makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly lower, risking objects on the approach or landing short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, by what height should an approach in IMC be stabilized, or you go around?
options: At the final approach fix
500 ft above airport elevation
200 ft above touchdown zone elevation
1,000 ft above airport elevation
quiz.why: Typically go around if not stabilized by 1,000 ft above airport elevation in IMC, or 500 ft in VMC [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: You lost 15 knots on short final. What is the best way to report it?
options: "Negative wind shear on final, 15 knots at 300 feet"
"Wind shear, loss of 15 knots at 300 feet"
"Moderate turbulence, loss of 15 knots on final"
"Positive wind shear, 15 knots at 300 feet, use caution"
quiz.why: Don't use "negative" or "positive"; give the airspeed gain or loss and the altitude [[34:106|AIM 7-1-22]].

quiz.q: After landing, when is your airplane clear of the runway?
options: When the nosewheel and main gear cross the runway edge line onto the taxiway
When you have turned onto the taxiway centerline lead-off line
When the tower tells you to contact ground control on the radio
When all parts of the airplane cross the holding position markings
quiz.why: You are not clear of the runway until all parts of the airplane have crossed the holding position markings [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a]] [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21b]].

quiz.q: Which approach lighting system does the chart list for runway 17C?
options: ALSF-1
MALSF
ALSF-2
MALSR
quiz.why: The strip's lighting box for Rwy 17C reads ALSF-2. The box with the system name and icon is in the middle briefing strip [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]] [[29:185|IPH Figure 4-24]].

quiz.q: Which approach lighting system does the chart list for runway 17R?
options: MALSR
REIL
ALSF-2
ODALS
quiz.why: The box for Rwy 17R reads MALSR with an A5 icon [[29:185|IPH Figure 4-24]].

quiz.q: Where on an approach chart do you find the approach lighting system name?
options: In the communications strip along the top
In the middle strip beside the notes box
In the minimums box at the bottom
In the airport sketch notes box only
quiz.why: The middle briefing strip holds the notes box, the approach lighting system box and the missed approach text [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]].

quiz.q: On the airport sketch, which runways have runway end identifier lights?
options: 15R and 33L
All runways
10 and 33L
15L and 33R
quiz.why: The note reads REIL Rwys 15L and 33R [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

quiz.q: On the airport sketch, which runways have touchdown zone and centerline lights?
options: 15R and 33R
15L and 33R
10 and 33L
All runways
quiz.why: The note reads TDZL/RCLS Rwys 10 and 33L. Runway centerline lights are shown by a negative dot pattern through the runway [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

quiz.q: You are at the MDA with the approach lights in sight. You see no red bars and no other part of the runway. How low may you go using only the approach lights?
options: All the way to touchdown
To 50 feet above the TDZE
To 100 feet above the TDZE
To 200 feet above the TDZE
quiz.why: 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i) says you may not descend below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation using the approach lights unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also in sight [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

takeaways: Below DA or MDA you need all three: normal descent position, flight visibility, and a distinct runway reference.
Approach lights alone take you to 100 ft above TDZE, no lower, unless you see red bars.
Leave the MDA at the VDP, not before. No VDP? Height above TDZE ÷ 300 = NM out.
Stabilized by 1,000 ft in IMC: on path, on speed (+10/-5), 500-1,000 fpm, configured. If not, go around.
Night, rain, haze, narrow runways and dark terrain push you low. Trust the glideslope, VGSI and altimeter.
Fast, high or long eats runway: 10% fast = 20% longer; 50 ft high = 1,000 ft longer.
Go-around: power, attitude, configuration. Landing expectancy and pride are the enemy.
cfi_notes: The IFH list of 91.175(c) references (IFH 10-21) omits the 100 ft approach light limit and calls the VGSI a VASI. Teach the current 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i) wording [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

Neither the AIM text nor the IFH names the red bars; IFH Figure 9-36 and AIM FIG 2-1-1 only draw them. The names "red terminating bars" and "red side row bars" come from 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i). Point out where each sits in the figure, and that an ALSF-2 run as an SSALR in good weather shows no red [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]] [[33:122|AIM FIG 2-1-1]].
The IFH says the second glidepath of a three-bar VASI is "about 25 percent higher"; the current AIM says normally 1/4 degree higher. Use the AIM [[23:281|IFH 9-38]] [[33:121|AIM 2-1-2]].

The IFH still says A/FD; it is now the Chart Supplement [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]]. The IFH inoperative-ALS example and its table values are older samples, not rules to memorize [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. Teach students to read the chart notes and NOTAMs first, then the current TPP front matter [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j REFERENCE]].

IPH 4-39 is written for two-pilot crews (PF/PM). Adapt it for single pilot: the student flies instruments with brief outside glances, and the autopilot can act as a "second pilot" for the runway search.
Examiners often ask: what can you see at DA and go lower? Use a MALSR (no red bars) to test the 100 ft rule, and ask what flight visibility means versus reported visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].
Common student error: diving for the runway at the MAP on a nonprecision approach. Use the VDP and the 300 ft per NM check in every lesson [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
Use view-limiting device removal at minimums with partial-panel scan glances, not a sudden full switch to outside, so the student learns a gradual transition.
gaps: The ACS gives no numeric tolerances for IR.VI.E; the sources give criteria (AFH stabilized approach) but no checkride limits.
Airplane-specific approach speeds, flap settings, landing and go-around checklists and landing distance charts come from the POH/AFM, which is not in these sources.
AC 00-54 (Pilot Wind Shear Guide), referenced by the PHAK for wind shear recognition and escape, is not available; no light-airplane wind shear escape procedure is taught here.
The TPP Inoperative Components or Visual Aids Table and the TPP circling radius table (page B2) are not in these sources.

activities.title: Read the approach lights
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: Read the runway
activities.intro: Tap a marking or light, then tap what it tells you.

pairs.r: Two broad white stripes about 1,000 ft from the threshold
Bar pairs that give distance in 500 ft steps
Last 2,000 ft, or last half, of an instrument runway
The threshold, as seen by a landing airplane

pairs.l: Pulsing white lights across the runway
pairs.r: LAHSO hold short point, on while LAHSO is in effect

activities.title: Work the nonprecision profile
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: FAF altitude 2,200 ft MSL, TDZE 400 ft, 2.5 minutes from the FAF to the runway. What descent rate gets you down on time (fpm)?
MDA 1,000 ft MSL, TDZE 550 ft, no VDP. How many NM from the threshold should you leave the MDA on a 3° path?
items.why: Height above TDZE 450 ft ÷ 300 ft per NM = 1.5 NM [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

items.q: You are 3.5 NM from the threshold. TDZE is 300 ft. What altitude MSL puts you on a 3° glidepath?
The chart minimum is RVR 2000 and RVR is not reported. What visibility do you need, in statute miles?
items.why: Use the next higher RVR value, 2400, which is 1/2 SM. Do not interpolate [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]].

activities.title: Which way does the illusion push you?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: You tend to fly too LOW
You tend to fly too HIGH

items.t: Runway narrower than you are used to
Runway wider than you are used to
Dark water or snow on final (black hole)
Bright runway lights with few lights around

activities.title: True or false: wind shear and landing distance
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A headwind that suddenly changes to a tailwind lowers your airspeed and performance.
cards.why: True. Headwind to tailwind decreases airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

cards.s: Microbursts are easy to spot on conventional weather radar.
cards.why: False. Small size, short life and little rain make them hard to detect [[34:107|AIM 7-1-24]].

cards.s: Crossing the threshold at 100 ft instead of 50 ft adds about 1,000 ft to the landing distance.
cards.why: True. Each 10 ft above 50 ft adds about 200 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

cards.s: Being 10% fast on final adds only about 10% to the landing distance.
cards.why: False. The rule of thumb is about 20% [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].

cards.s: When landing behind a larger airplane, stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point.
cards.why: True. That keeps you above its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: Reporting "negative wind shear on final" clearly tells others you lost airspeed.
cards.why: False. It has been taken to mean no wind shear. Report the airspeed change and altitude [[34:106|AIM 7-1-22]].

activities.title: From minimums to clear of the runway
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Brief DA/MDA, VDP, lighting and the missed approach
Be stabilized and configured by 1,000 ft above the airport
At DA, or at MDA by the VDP, check the three 91.175(c) tests
Descend visually on the glideslope or VGSI to the aiming point
Touch down in the touchdown zone
Exit at the first available taxiway
Stop past the hold line, then run the after-landing checklist

activities.title: Night ILS: decide at each step
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a Cessna 172, on the ILS at night. The runway has a MALSR and a 4-light PAPI. The chart visibility minimum is 1/2 SM and the tower reports 3/4 SM in mist. The airport sits in dark farmland.

steps.s: Approach asks you to keep 120 knots to the final approach fix. That would leave you fast and clean at 1,000 ft above the airport.
options: Tell ATC you are unable; it would make the approach unstable
Accept the speed and plan to slow down and configure below 500 ft
Accept and descend steeply later to make up the lost time
Accept and skip the landing checklist to save time on final
steps.why: Tell ATC when an instruction would make the approach unstable because of speed or descent rate [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]]. You need to be stabilized by 1,000 ft in IMC [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: Inside the FAF the tower clears you to land: "caution wake turbulence, Boeing 737 landed ahead on the same runway."
options: Fly slightly below the glidepath and land short of its touchdown point
Land at the 737's touchdown point
Slow 10 knots below approach speed to add spacing
Stay on or above the 737's path and land beyond its touchdown point
steps.why: Behind a larger airplane landing on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

steps.s: At the DA you see only the approach lights. Flight visibility looks about 3/4 mile.
options: Go missed; approach lights alone are not a 91.175 visual reference
Level off at the DA and keep looking for the runway environment
Continue to touchdown using only the approach lights as reference
Continue below DA, but not below 100 ft above TDZE without another reference
steps.why: The ALS is a reference, but a MALSR has no red bars, so on it alone you may not go below 100 ft above TDZE [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]] [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]].

steps.s: At 150 ft above TDZE the threshold and runway lights appear. The PAPI shows four red, but the runway looks normal to you.
options: Trust what you see and reduce power to continue the descent
Add power and raise the nose to get back on the glidepath
Raise the flaps to reduce drag and flatten the approach
Push the nose over to reach the runway sooner and save time
steps.why: Four red is low [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]]. Dark terrain makes you feel higher than you are [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Add power and pitch; never raise flaps to fix an undershoot [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: Back on the glidepath at 80 ft, a vehicle's lights move onto the runway ahead.
options: Land and brake hard to stop short of the vehicle
Land long, and roll out past the vehicle on the runway
Go around: power, attitude, configuration
S-turn on short final to buy time for it to clear
steps.why: A vehicle or other hazard on the runway calls for a rejected landing [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. Go-around order: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

activities.title: Find it on the airport sketch
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

final_quiz.q: The approach chart lists a visibility minimum of RVR 1800, but RVR is not reported for the runway. What visibility do you need?
options: 1/4 SM
1/2 SM
3/8 SM
5/8 SM
final_quiz.why: Between listed values, use the next higher RVR: 1800 becomes 2400, which is 1/2 SM [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)]].

final_quiz.q: Flying an ILS to a runway with an ALSF-1, you see the red terminating bars at DA, but nothing else of the runway yet. What does 91.175 allow?
options: Continue only down to 100 ft above TDZE, then go missed unless the runway is in sight
Continue below 100 ft above TDZE if visibility and position also meet the rule
Go missed; the approach lights are not enough, you need the runway itself in sight
Level off at DA until the threshold or runway lights appear in view
final_quiz.why: The approach lights are a reference, and with red terminating bars distinctly visible the 100 ft limit no longer applies [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. The ALSF-1's red bars just before the threshold are its red terminating bars [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]].

final_quiz.q: Circling at the MDA, a patch of cloud hides the whole airport. The bank angle is normal. What do you do?
options: Hold altitude and keep circling until the cloud passes by the field
Descend a little to get below the cloud and regain sight of the runway
Go missed, with the first climbing turn toward the landing runway
Continue the turn at the MDA; it is only a normal bank issue
final_quiz.why: If an identifiable part of the airport is not visible while circling, for a reason other than normal bank, go missed [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. Make the first climbing turn toward the landing runway [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

final_quiz.q: FAF altitude 2,400 ft MSL, TDZE 600 ft, 3 minutes from FAF to the runway. Using the IPH method, what descent rate do you plan?
options: 600 fpm
800 fpm
500 fpm
900 fpm

final_quiz.q: A straight-in LNAV approach has an MDA of 1,180 ft MSL and a TDZE of 580 ft, but no VDP. About how far from the threshold should you start down from the MDA?
options: About 2.0 NM
About 1.5 NM
About 1.0 NM
About 3.0 NM
final_quiz.why: Height above TDZE is 600 ft. On a 3° path that is 300 ft per NM, so 600 ÷ 300 = 2.0 NM [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

final_quiz.q: The tower reports 1 SM, and the chart minimum is 1 SM. At the DA you see the runway lights, but you judge flight visibility at about 1/2 SM. What does the rule say?
options: Land, because you see the runway lights
Land, since the reported visibility is at minimums
You may not land; go missed
Continue to 100 ft and then decide
final_quiz.why: Flight visibility must not be less than the chart value to go below DA or land. Only you can judge it, and you go missed regardless of the report [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]] [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH approach speed is 66 knots. The wind is 12 gusting 20 knots. Using the AFH guidance, what speed do you fly?
options: 66 knots
74 knots
86 knots
70 knots
final_quiz.why: Gust factor 20 - 12 = 8 knots; add half, 4 knots: 70 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your normal landing distance is 1,200 ft. You cross the threshold 10% faster than the recommended speed. About how much distance do you need?
final_quiz.why: 10% fast adds about 20%: 1,200 × 1.2 = 1,440 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. 1,320 ft is the common mistake of adding only 10%.

final_quiz.q: You cross the threshold at 80 ft instead of 50 ft. About how much does your landing distance grow?
options: About 1,000 ft
About 300 ft
About 600 ft
About 150 ft
final_quiz.why: 30 ft too high at 200 ft per 10 ft = about 600 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

final_quiz.q: Night approach to a lighted runway with dark, unlit country all around. The runway lights are bright. Which illusion should you expect?
options: Fog illusion, making you pitch up and steepen the approach
A wide runway illusion, making you flare low and land short
Upslope, making you fly a lower approach and land short of it
Bright lights making the runway seem closer, so you fly higher
final_quiz.why: Bright runway and approach lights with few lights around can make the runway seem closer, so you fly a higher approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5b3(f)]]. Overflying dark terrain can also lead to a low approach, so use the VGSI [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5b3(f)]].

final_quiz.q: A Boeing 757 lands just ahead of you on the same runway. How do you avoid its wake?
options: Fly just below its path and land well before its touchdown point
Stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point
Fly 200 ft below its path and land long past its touchdown point
Fly its exact path and land right at its touchdown point
final_quiz.why: Landing behind a larger airplane on the same runway: stay at or above its final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: On short final you are below the glidepath and the airspeed is right. Which correction does the AFH recommend?
options: Raise the flaps one notch to reduce drag and flatten the descent
Add power and raise the nose, leveling off until you meet the path
Pull the nose up without adding power, and trade airspeed for altitude
Reduce power and lower the nose to keep the airspeed constant
final_quiz.why: If low, increase pitch and add power to level off until you meet the glide path. Raising flaps can cause a sudden sink, and pitch alone is a common error [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists an unfactored dry landing distance of 1,500 ft. Using the AC 91-79B factor for a reciprocating airplane on a dry runway, what is the landing distance required?
options: About 2,505 ft
About 3,450 ft
About 1,725 ft
About 3,900 ft
final_quiz.why: 1,500 × 1.67 = 2,505 ft. The factor already includes a 15% safety margin [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. 1,725 ft adds only the 15%.

final_quiz.q: Which lights does the sketch note list for all runways?
options: HIRL
TDZL
REIL
RCLS
final_quiz.why: The note reads HIRL all rwys. Runway lights are listed in a note at the bottom of the sketch [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

final_quiz.q: How does the chart show an approach light system on the airport sketch?
options: As a symbol at the end of the lighted runway
As a dashed line along the profile view
Only in the Chart Supplement, not on the chart
As a note in the communications strip at the top
final_quiz.why: Other approach lighting is shown as a symbol on the side of the runway where it is located [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

final_quiz.q: The table under the sketch is for a 3.5 NM run from the FAF to the MAP. How long at 120 knots?
final_quiz.why: At 120 knots the table reads 1:45 [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a visual reference that 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3) lets you use to continue below the DA or MDA?
options: Runway end identifier lights
The blue taxiway edge lights
The rotating airport beacon
The taxiway centerline lights
final_quiz.why: The list in 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3) includes the runway end identifier lights, the approach lights, the threshold, the touchdown zone and the runway or its markings or lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].
